Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2 of the matrix A=[5335].

a
13[2332]
b
12[1−1−11]
c
12[1221]
d
13[3−2−23]
e
[1111]
Submit

EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=2. Computing A−2I, we get

A−2I=[5335]−2[1001]=[3333].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[330330]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[330000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is

[−x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector

v=[−11],

where ‖v‖=2. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=12[−11]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=12[−11]⋅12[−11]=12[−11]⋅[−11]=12[1−1−11].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Projection Matrix That Orthogonally Projects a Vector to the Subspace Spanned by an Eigenvector

solution.reasoning: Solving (A−2I)v=0 gives 3v₁+3v₂=0, so the eigenspace is spanned by v=(1,−1)ᵀ. Since vᵀv=2, its orthogonal projection matrix is P=vvᵀ/(vᵀv)=(1/2)[[1,−1],[−1,1]], which is option b. This matrix fixes (1,−1)ᵀ and annihilates its orthogonal complement, spanned by (1,1)ᵀ. feedback.name: Question 11
feedback.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is

[−x2x2],x2∈R.

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{17}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2 of the matrix A=[3−4−418].

a
117[16441]
b
117[1−4−416]
c
117[1−4−416]
d
17[16441]
e
117[16441]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=2. Computing A−2I, we get

A−2I=[3−4−418]−2[1−4−416]=[1−4−416].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[1−40−4160]R2:=R2+4R1∼[1−40000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=4x2. Hence, the general solution is

[4x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector

v=[41],

where ‖v‖=17. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=117[41]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=117[41]⋅117[41]=117[41]⋅[41]=117[16441].

The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{17}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2 of the matrix A=[3−4−418].

a
117[16441]
b
117[1−4−416]
c
117[1−4−416]
d
17[16441]
e
117[16441]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=2. Computing A−2I, we get

A−2I=[3−4−418]−2[1−4−416]=[1−4−416].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[1−40−4160]R2:=R2+4R1∼[1−40000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=4x2. Hence, the general solution is

[4x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector

v=[41],

where ‖v‖=17. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=117[41]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=117[41]⋅117[41]=117[41]⋅[41]=117[16441].

This matrix fixes v and annihilates the perpendicular vector (1,−4)ᵀ. \begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{17}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 13
?

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−1 of the matrix A=[8663].

a
113[4−6−69]
b
113[9664]
c
113[4−6−69]
d
113[−944−6]
e
13[9664]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=−1. Computing A−(−1)I, we get

A+I=[8663]+[1001]=[9664].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[960640]R2:=R2+(−23)R1∼[960000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−23x2. Hence, the general solution is

[−23x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=3, we get the eigenvector

v=[−23],

where ‖v‖=13. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=113[−23]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=113[−23]⋅113[−23]=113[−23]⋅[−23]=113[4−6−69].

last_observation.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−1 of the matrix A=[8663].

a
113[4−6−69]
b
113[9664]
c
113[4−6−69]
d
113[−944−6]
e
13[9664]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=−1. Computing A−(−1)I, we get

A+I=[8663]+[1001]=[9664].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[960640]R2:=R2+(−23)R1∼[960000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−23x2. Hence, the general solution is

[−23x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=3, we get the eigenvector

v=[−23],

where ‖v‖=13. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=113[−23]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=113[−23]⋅113[−23]=113[−23]⋅[−23]=113[4−6−69].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Projection Matrix That Orthogonally Projects a Vector to the Subspace Spanned by an Eigenvector

solution.reasoning: Solving (A+I)v=0 gives 9v₁+6v₂=0, so the eigenspace is spanned by v=(2,−3)ᵀ. Since vᵀv=13, the orthogonal projection is P=vvᵀ/(vᵀv)=(1/13)[[4,−6],[−6,9]], option c. It fixes v and annihilates the perpendicular vector (3,2)ᵀ. The supplied worked example concerns a different matrix, so it does not establish Math Academy's answer key for the current question.

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =5.$ Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =5.$ Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=5 of the matrix A=[1224].

a
15[1224]
b
15[1224]
c
15[−4−1−12]
d
[4221]
e
15[4221]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=5. Computing A−5I, we get

A−5I=[1224]−5[1001]=[−422−1].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−420210]R2:=R2+12R1∼[−420000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=12x2. Hence, the general solution is

[12x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=2, we get the eigenvector

v=[12],

where ‖v‖=5. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=15[12]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=15[12]⋅15[12]=15[12]⋅[12]=15[1224].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Projection Matrix That Orthogonally Projects a Vector to the Subspace Spanned by an Eigenvector

solution.reasoning: Solving (A−5I)v=0 gives −4v₁+2v₂=0, so the eigenspace is spanned by v=(1,2)ᵀ. Since vᵀv=5, the orthogonal projection is P=vvᵀ/(vᵀv)=(1/5)[[1,2],[2,4]], option b. It fixes v and annihilates the perpendicular vector (2,−1)ᵀ. The supplied example yields the same projection for a different matrix and eigenvalue, but does not establish Math Academy's current answer key.

feedback.name: Question 14
feedback.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =5.$ Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=5 of the matrix A=[1224].

a
15[1224]
b
15[1224]
c
15[−4−1−12]
d
[4221]
e
15[4221]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=5. Computing A−5I, we get

A−5I=[1224]−5[1001]=[−422−1].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−420210]R2:=R2+12R1∼[−420000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=12x2. Hence, the general solution is

[12x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=2, we get the eigenvector

v=[12],

where ‖v‖=5. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=15[12]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=15[12]⋅15[12]=15[12]⋅[12]=15[1224].

question.name: Question 15
question.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =8$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =8.$ Computing $A-8I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ -5 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=8 of the matrix A=[3−5−53].

a
12[−111−1]
b
12[1−1−11]
c
[1111]
d
12[1−1−11]
e
12[−111−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=8. Computing A−8I, we get

A−8I=[3−5−53]−8[1001]=[−5−5−5−5].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−5−50−5−50]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[−5−50000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is

[−x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector

v=[−11],

where ‖v‖=2. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=12[−11]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=12[−11]⋅12[−11]=12[−11]⋅[−11]=12[1−1−11].

last_observation.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =8.$ Computing $A-8I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ -5 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=8 of the matrix A=[3−5−53].

a
12[−111−1]
b
12[1−1−11]
c
[1111]

12[1−1−11]

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=8. Computing A−8I, we get

A−8I=[3−5−53]−8[1001]=[−5−5−5−5].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−5−50−5−50]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[−5−50000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is

[−x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector

v=[−11],

where ‖v‖=2. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=12[−11]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=12[−11]⋅12[−11]=12[−11]⋅[−11]=12[1−1−11].
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Projection Matrix That Orthogonally Projects a Vector to the Subspace Spanned by an Eigenvector

solution.reasoning: Solving (A−8I)v=0 gives v₁+v₂=0, so the eigenspace is spanned by v=(1,−1)ᵀ. Since vᵀv=2, its orthogonal projection matrix is P=vvᵀ/(vᵀv)=(1/2)[[1,−1],[−1,1]], option b. It fixes v and annihilates the perpendicular vector (1,1)ᵀ. feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =8$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =8.$ Computing $A-8I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ -5 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 15
?

Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps x∈R2 onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=8 of the matrix A=[3−5−53].

a
12[−111−1]
b
12[1−1−11]
c
[1111]
d
12[1−1−11]
e
12[−111−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The spectral decomposition of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A is given by

A=λ1u1⋅u1T+λ2u2⋅u2T, where u1 and u2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A corresponding to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2, respectively.

Moreover, ui⋅uiT is the projection matrix corresponding to ui.

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ=8. Computing A−8I, we get

A−8I=[3−5−53]−8[1001]=[−5−5−5−5].

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−5−50−5−50]R2:=R2+(−1)R1∼[−5−50000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain x1=−x2. Hence, the general solution is

[−x2x2],x2∈R.

Therefore, setting x2=1, we get the eigenvector

v=[−11],

where ‖v‖=2. Dividing v by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: u=v‖v‖=12[−11]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

u⋅uT=12[−11]⋅12[−11]=12[−11]⋅[−11]=12[1−1−11].

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[5X-2Y].$

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. | $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=0$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.4$ | | $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ | | ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ | $0.45$ | $1$ | Therefore, the probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y$ are given by the following tables:
$x$ $0$ $1$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.4$ $0.6$

$y$ $0$ $1$ $2$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.3$ $0.25$ $0.45$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =0\cdot 0.4+1\cdot 0.6 \\ & =0+0.6 \\ & =0.6\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 0.45 \\ & =0+0.25+0.9 \\ & =1.15.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X-2Y] & =5\,\text{E}[X]-2\,\text{E}[Y] \\ & =5(0.6)-2(1.15) \\ & =3-2.3 \\ & =0.7.\end{aligned} $$

| $X=3$ | $0.15$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ |

| $x$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{X}(x)$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-1)\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.3 \\  & =-0.3+0.4+0.9 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[2X-3Y].$

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.15$ | $0.15$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. | $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | ${f}_{X}$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.1$ | $0.35$ | | $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.15$ | $0.35$ | | $X=4$ | $0.15$ | $0.15$ | $0.3$ | | ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.6$ | $0.4$ | $1$ | Therefore, the probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y$ are given by the following tables:
$x$ $1$ $2$ $4$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.35$ $0.35$ $0.3$

$y$ $2$ $3$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.6$ $0.4$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =1\cdot 0.35+2\cdot 0.35+4\cdot 0.3 \\ & =0.35+0.7+1.2 \\ & =2.25\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =2\cdot 0.6+3\cdot 0.4 \\ & =1.2+1.2 \\ & =2.4.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-3Y] & =2\,\text{E}[X]-3\,\text{E}[Y] \\ & =2(2.25)-3(2.4) \\ & =4.5-7.2 \\ & =-2.7.\end{aligned} $$

questions.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[Y-X].$

| $f$ | $Y=-1$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |

questions.worked_solution:

$x$ $1$ $2$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.5$ $0.5$

$y$ $-1$ $1$ $2$ $4$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.25$ $0.15$ $0.35$ $0.25$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\ & =0.5+1 \\ & =1.5\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =(-1)\cdot 0.25+1\cdot 0.15+2\cdot 0.35+4\cdot 0.25 \\ & =-0.25+0.15+0.7+1 \\ & =1.6.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y-X] & =\text{E}[Y]-\,\text{E}[X] \\ & =1.6-1.5 \\ & =0.1.\end{aligned} $$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}(x+2y), & 1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{17}{30},$ find $\text{E}[X+2Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $1\le x\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{5}(x+2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[xy+{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(x+1-0) \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{2(x+1)}{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{8}{3}+2-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{23}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X+2Y] & =\text{E}[X]+2\text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{23}{15}+2(\frac{17}{30}) \\  & =\frac{23}{15}+\frac{17}{15} \\  & =\frac{40}{15} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{7}(x+\sqrt{y}), & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{4}{7},$ find $\text{E}[2X+Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{6}{7}(x+\sqrt{y})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{7}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x\sqrt{y}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{6}{7}(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}(2\sqrt{y}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{3}{7}(2\sqrt{y}+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{7}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{3/2}+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{7}{[\frac{4}{5}{y}^{5/2}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}(\frac{4}{5}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{39}{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X+Y] & =2\,\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[Y] \\  & =2(\frac{4}{7})+(\frac{39}{70}) \\  & =\frac{80+39}{70} \\  & =\frac{17}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y\sqrt{x}}{3}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 3, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{5},$ find $\text{E}[5X-Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{y\sqrt{x}}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{y}{3}{[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{y}{3}(\frac{2}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{2y}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}y\cdot \frac{2y}{9}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(9-0) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X-Y] & =5\,\text{E}[X]+(-1)\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =5(\frac{3}{5})+(-1)(2) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}xy, & 0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{2}{3},$ find $\text{E}[X+Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $0\le x\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}xy\,\text{d}y \\  & =x{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{x}{2}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+y}{21}, & -3\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=0,$ find $\text{E}[3X+7Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}+y}{21}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{21}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+xy]}_{x=-3}^{x=3} \\  & =\frac{1}{21}[(\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}+3y)-(\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}-3y)] \\  & =\frac{1}{21}[18+6y] \\  & =\frac{2(3+y)}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(3+y)}{7}.\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{7}{\int }_{0}^{1}3y+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{7}{[\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{7}(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{7}\cdot \frac{11}{6} \\  & =\frac{11}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[3X+7Y] & =3\,\text{E}[X]+7\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =3(0)+7(\frac{11}{21}) \\  & =0+\frac{11}{3} \\  & =\frac{11}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Expected Value of a Discrete Random Variable From a Joint Distribution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. | $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=5$ | $f_X$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=-1$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.35$ | | $X=2$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.35$ | | $X=4$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | | $f_Y$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $1$ | Therefore, the probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y$ are given by the following tables:
$x$ $-1$ $2$ $4$
$f_X(x)$ $0.35$ $0.35$ $0.3$

$y$ $0$ $1$ $3$ $5$
$f_Y(y)$ $0.3$ $0.2$ $0.2$ $0.3$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =(-1)\cdot 0.35+2\cdot 0.35+4\cdot 0.3 \\ & =-0.35+0.7+1.2 \\ & =1.55\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.2+3\cdot 0.2+5\cdot 0.3 \\ & =0+0.2+0.6+1.5 \\ & =2.3\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X-3Y] & =4\text{E}[X]-3\,\text{E}[Y] \\ & =4(1.55)-3(2.3) \\ & =6.2-6.9 \\ & =-0.7.\end{aligned} $$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Expected Value of a Continuous Random Variable From a Joint Distribution
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14155126/assets/f5e1e2931a6ad6c4b5751d67e325cc0aca6cbae85200e5d2fbd6f60ea28c899c.svg)

Find the expected value of $Y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The marginal density function for $Y$ when $y \geq 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{x}^{3}{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}{lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}{lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}{lim}_{b\to \infty }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{b}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14155126/assets/4dcb0094faeee6f3f155eb2e7a87c24cfb976c3f860f30b13cd7da61512544b2.svg)

Finally, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }y\cdot \frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{y}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }(1-\frac{1}{b}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To compute the expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ given a joint mass function $f(x,y),$ we must first find its marginal mass function $f_X.$ Once the marginal mass function is known, we can then compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ using the formula

$$
\textrm{E}[X]
= \sum\limits_{i=1}^n x_i \, f_X(x_i).
$$

For example, consider the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ |

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Since we're only interested in the expected value of $X,$ let's compute the row totals only.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.20}$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.80}$ |

Therefore, the marginal mass function of $X$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f_X(x)$ | $0.20$ | $0.80$ |
|  |  |  |

We can now compute the expected value of $X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\  & =1\cdot 0.2+2\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.2+1.6 \\  & =1.8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\textrm{E}[X] = 1.8.$

$$
\textrm{E}[X]
= \int_{-\infty}^\infty x \cdot f_X(x)\,\textrm d x.
$$

Let's see an example.

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. | $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=5$ | $f_X$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=-1$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.35$ | | $X=2$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.35$ | | $X=4$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | | $f_Y$ | $0.3$ | $0.2$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $1$ | Therefore, the probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y$ are given by the following tables:
$x$ $-1$ $2$ $4$
$f_X(x)$ $0.35$ $0.35$ $0.3$

$y$ $0$ $1$ $3$ $5$
$f_Y(y)$ $0.3$ $0.2$ $0.2$ $0.3$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =(-1)\cdot 0.35+2\cdot 0.35+4\cdot 0.3 \\ & =-0.35+0.7+1.2 \\ & =1.55\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.2+3\cdot 0.2+5\cdot 0.3 \\ & =0+0.2+0.6+1.5 \\ & =2.3\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X-3Y] & =4\text{E}[X]-3\,\text{E}[Y] \\ & =4(1.55)-3(2.3) \\ & =6.2-6.9 \\ & =-0.7.\end{aligned} $$

EXPLANATION

Recall that the marginal distribution for X corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for Y corresponds to the column totals.

f Y=0 Y=1 Y=2 fX
X=0 0.05 0.1 0.25 0.4
X=1 0.25 0.15 0.2 0.6
fY 0.3 0.25 0.45 1

Therefore, the probability mass functions for X and Y are given by the following tables:

x 0 1
fX(x) 0.4 0.6

y 0 1 2
fY(y) 0.3 0.25 0.45

Now, we can compute the expected values for X and Y:

E[X]=∑i=1nxifX(xi)=0⋅0.4+1⋅0.6=0+0.6=0.6

E[Y]=∑i=1nyifY(yi)=0⋅0.3+1⋅0.25+2⋅0.45=0+0.25+0.9=1.15.

Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain

E[5X−2Y]=5E[X]−2E[Y]=5(0.6)−2(1.15)=3−2.3=0.7.

Question 3
?

Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables X and Y below, find E[2X−3Y].

f Y=2 Y=3
X=1 0.25 0.1
X=2 0.2 0.15
X=4 0.15 0.15
a
−4.3
b
−1.95
c
2.05
d
−2.7
e
11.55
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the marginal distribution for X corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for Y corresponds to the column totals.

f Y=2 Y=3 fX
X=1 0.25 0.1 0.35
X=2 0.2 0.15 0.35
X=4 0.15 0.15 0.3
fY 0.6 0.4 1

Therefore, the probability mass functions for X and Y are given by the following tables:

x 1 2 4
fX(x) 0.35 0.35 0.3

y 2 3
fY(y) 0.6 0.4

Now, we can compute the expected values for X and Y:

E[X]=∑i=1nxifX(xi)=1⋅0.35+2⋅0.35+4⋅0.3=0.35+0.7+1.2=2.25

E[Y]=∑i=1nyifY(yi)=2⋅0.6+3⋅0.4=1.2+1.2=2.4.

Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain

E[2X−3Y]=2E[X]−3E[Y]=2(2.25)−3(2.4)=4.5−7.2=−2.7.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals.

| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=4$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.2$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.05$ | $0.45$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.55$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $…$ | $…$ | $…$ | $…$ | $1$ |

Therefore, the probability mass function for  $X$ is given by the following table:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{X}(x)$ | $0.45$ | $0.55$ |

Finally, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.45+1\cdot 0.55 \\  & =0+0.55 \\  & =0.55.\end{aligned}
$$

x 1 2
fX(x) 0.5 0.5

y −1 1 2 4
fY(y) 0.25 0.15 0.35 0.25

tutorial.name: Continuous Random Variables
tutorial.problem:
To compute the expected value of a *continuous* random variable $X$ given a joint density function $f(x,y),$ we must first find its marginal density function $f_X.$ Once the marginal density function is known, we can then compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ using the formula

$$
\textrm{E}[X]
= \int_{-\infty}^\infty x \cdot f_X(x)\,\textrm d x.
$$

Let's see an example.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The marginal density function for $Y$ when $y \geq 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{x}^{3}{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}{lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}{lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}{lim}_{b\to \infty }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{b}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{4}{{y}^{3}}(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14155126/assets/f2eaf65338e3188fe2931d637a38cc02d63b86e1e948a30832dbf910c3ebaf54.svg)

Finally, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }y\cdot \frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{y}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }(1-\frac{1}{b}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We're given E[Y]. So, we first need to compute E[X].

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{6}{7}(x+\sqrt{y})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{7}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x\sqrt{y}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{6}{7}(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}(2\sqrt{y}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{3}{7}(2\sqrt{y}+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{7}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{3/2}+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{7}{[\frac{4}{5}{y}^{5/2}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}(\frac{4}{5}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{39}{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X+Y] & =2\,\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[Y] \\  & =2(\frac{4}{7})+(\frac{39}{70}) \\  & =\frac{80+39}{70} \\  & =\frac{17}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $0\le x\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}xy\,\text{d}y \\  & =x{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{x}{2}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X+Y] & =\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Expected Value of a Continuous Random Variable From a Joint Distribution
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}+y}{21}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{21}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+xy]}_{x=-3}^{x=3} \\  & =\frac{1}{21}[(\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}+3y)-(\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}-3y)] \\  & =\frac{1}{21}[18+6y] \\  & =\frac{2(3+y)}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(3+y)}{7}.\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{7}{\int }_{0}^{1}3y+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{7}{[\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{7}(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{7}\cdot \frac{11}{6} \\  & =\frac{11}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[3X+7Y] & =3\,\text{E}[X]+7\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =3(0)+7(\frac{11}{21}) \\  & =0+\frac{11}{3} \\  & =\frac{11}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[5X-2Y].$

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ |
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. | $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=0$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.4$ | | $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ | | ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ | $0.45$ | $1$ | Therefore, the probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y$ are given by the following tables:
$x$ $0$ $1$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.4$ $0.6$

$y$ $0$ $1$ $2$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.3$ $0.25$ $0.45$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =0\cdot 0.4+1\cdot 0.6 \\ & =0+0.6 \\ & =0.6\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 0.45 \\ & =0+0.25+0.9 \\ & =1.15.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X-2Y] & =5\,\text{E}[X]-2\,\text{E}[Y] \\ & =5(0.6)-2(1.15) \\ & =3-2.3 \\ & =0.7.\end{aligned} $$

Question 1

Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables X and Y below, find E[5X−2Y].

f Y=0 Y=1 Y=2
X=0 0.05 0.1 0.25
X=1 0.25 0.15 0.2
a
1.7
b
1.5
c
0.6
d
1.15
e
0.7
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the marginal distribution for X corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for Y corresponds to the column totals.

f Y=0 Y=1 Y=2 fX
X=0 0.05 0.1 0.25 0.4
X=1 0.25 0.15 0.2 0.6
fY 0.3 0.25 0.45 1

Therefore, the probability mass functions for X and Y are given by the following tables:

x 0 1
fX(x) 0.4 0.6

y 0 1 2
fY(y) 0.3 0.25 0.45

Now, we can compute the expected values for X and Y:

E[X]=∑i=1nxifX(xi)=0⋅0.4+1⋅0.6=0+0.6=0.6

E[Y]=∑i=1nyifY(yi)=0⋅0.3+1⋅0.25+2⋅0.45=0+0.25+0.9=1.15.

Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain

E[5X−2Y]=5E[X]−2E[Y]=5(0.6)−2(1.15)=3−2.3=0.7.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[X].$

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=-1$ | $0.05$ | $0.05$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.1$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.15$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ |
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals.

| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=-1$ | $0.05$ | $0.05$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.1$ | $0.15$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.15$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $…$ | $…$ | $…$ | $1$ |

Therefore, the probability mass function for  $X$ is given by the following table:

| $x$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{X}(x)$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ | $0.3$ |

Finally, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-1)\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.3 \\  & =-0.3+0.4+0.9 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[2X-3Y].$

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.1$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.15$ | $0.15$ |
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. | $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | ${f}_{X}$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.1$ | $0.35$ | | $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.15$ | $0.35$ | | $X=4$ | $0.15$ | $0.15$ | $0.3$ | | ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.6$ | $0.4$ | $1$ | Therefore, the probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y$ are given by the following tables:
$x$ $1$ $2$ $4$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.35$ $0.35$ $0.3$

$y$ $2$ $3$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.6$ $0.4$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =1\cdot 0.35+2\cdot 0.35+4\cdot 0.3 \\ & =0.35+0.7+1.2 \\ & =2.25\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =2\cdot 0.6+3\cdot 0.4 \\ & =1.2+1.2 \\ & =2.4.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-3Y] & =2\,\text{E}[X]-3\,\text{E}[Y] \\ & =2(2.25)-3(2.4) \\ & =4.5-7.2 \\ & =-2.7.\end{aligned} $$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[X].$

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.2$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.05$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ |
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals.

| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=4$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.2$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.05$ | $0.45$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.55$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $…$ | $…$ | $…$ | $…$ | $1$ |

Therefore, the probability mass function for  $X$ is given by the following table:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{X}(x)$ | $0.45$ | $0.55$ |

Finally, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.45+1\cdot 0.55 \\  & =0+0.55 \\  & =0.55.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[Y-X].$

| $f$ | $Y=-1$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.1$ |
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. | $f$ | $Y=-1$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | ${f}_{X}$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.15$ | $0.5$ | | $X=2$ | $0.2$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $0.1$ | $0.5$ | | ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.35$ | $0.25$ | $1$ | Therefore, the probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y$ are given by the following tables:
$x$ $1$ $2$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.5$ $0.5$

$y$ $-1$ $1$ $2$ $4$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.25$ $0.15$ $0.35$ $0.25$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\ & =0.5+1 \\ & =1.5\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =(-1)\cdot 0.25+1\cdot 0.15+2\cdot 0.35+4\cdot 0.25 \\ & =-0.25+0.15+0.7+1 \\ & =1.6.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y-X] & =\text{E}[Y]-\,\text{E}[X] \\ & =1.6-1.5 \\ & =0.1.\end{aligned} $$

Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables X and Y below, find E[Y−X].

f Y=−1 Y=1 Y=2 Y=4
X=1 0.05 0.1 0.2 0.15
X=2 0.2 0.05 0.15 0.1
a
1.3
b
0.5
c
2.1
d
0.1

1.8

EXPLANATION

Recall that the marginal distribution for X corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for Y corresponds to the column totals.

f Y=−1 Y=1 Y=2 Y=4 fX
X=1 0.05 0.1 0.2 0.15 0.5
X=2 0.2 0.05 0.15 0.1 0.5
fY 0.25 0.15 0.35 0.25 1

Therefore, the probability mass functions for X and Y are given by the following tables:

x 1 2
fX(x) 0.5 0.5

y −1 1 2 4
fY(y) 0.25 0.15 0.35 0.25

Now, we can compute the expected values for X and Y:

E[X]=∑i=1nxifX(xi)=1⋅0.5+2⋅0.5=0.5+1=1.5

E[Y]=∑i=1nyifY(yi)=(−1)⋅0.25+1⋅0.15+2⋅0.35+4⋅0.25=−0.25+0.15+0.7+1=1.6.

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =1\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.5 \\ & =0.5+1 \\ & =1.5\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =(-1)\cdot 0.25+1\cdot 0.15+2\cdot 0.35+4\cdot 0.25 \\ & =-0.25+0.15+0.7+1 \\ & =1.6.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y-X] & =\text{E}[Y]-\,\text{E}[X] \\ & =1.6-1.5 \\ & =0.1.\end{aligned} $$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}(x+2y), & 1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{17}{30},$ find $\text{E}[X+2Y].$
question.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $1\le x\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{5}(x+2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[xy+{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(x+1-0) \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{2(x+1)}{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{8}{3}+2-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{23}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X+2Y] & =\text{E}[X]+2\text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{23}{15}+2(\frac{17}{30}) \\  & =\frac{23}{15}+\frac{17}{15} \\  & =\frac{40}{15} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Let X and Y be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function f(x,y)={25(x+2y),1≤x≤2,0≤y≤1,0,otherwise. Given that E[Y]=1730, find E[X+2Y].

a
83
b
74
c
92
d
115
e
94
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We're given E[Y]. So, we first need to compute E[X].

The marginal density function for X when 1≤x≤2 is fX(x)=∫−∞∞f(x,y)dy=∫0125(x+2y)dy=25[xy+y2]y=0y=1=25(x+1−0)=2(x+1)5.

Therefore, the expected value of X is E[X]=∫−∞∞xfX(x)dx=∫12x⋅2(x+1)5dx=25∫12(x2+x)dx=25[x33+x22]12=25(83+2−13−12)=2315.

Finally, we obtain

E[X+2Y]=E[X]+2E[Y]=2315+2(1730)=2315+1715=4015=83.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}(x+2y), & 1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{17}{30},$ find $\text{E}[X+2Y].$
feedback.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $1\le x\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{5}(x+2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[xy+{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(x+1-0) \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{2(x+1)}{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{8}{3}+2-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{23}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X+2Y] & =\text{E}[X]+2\text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{23}{15}+2(\frac{17}{30}) \\  & =\frac{23}{15}+\frac{17}{15} \\  & =\frac{40}{15} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{7}(x+\sqrt{y}), & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{4}{7},$ find $\text{E}[2X+Y].$
question.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{6}{7}(x+\sqrt{y})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{7}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x\sqrt{y}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{6}{7}(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}(2\sqrt{y}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{3}{7}(2\sqrt{y}+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{7}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{3/2}+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{7}{[\frac{4}{5}{y}^{5/2}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}(\frac{4}{5}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{39}{70}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X+Y] & =2\,\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[Y] \\  & =2(\frac{4}{7})+(\frac{39}{70}) \\  & =\frac{80+39}{70} \\  & =\frac{17}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$
