question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=1$ for the curve $r(t)=⟨t,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}(1)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(1)$ and ${r}^{″}(1)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨1,1,0⟩\times ⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & \,\,-1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, the radius of the osculating circle at  $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}=\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}{\,1\,}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}(1)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(1)$ and ${r}^{″}(1)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨1,1,0⟩\times ⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & \,\,-1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, the radius of the osculating circle at  $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}=\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}{\,1\,}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨0,-{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ and ${r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-2,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-2\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖} \\  & =\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\pi $ for the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times 2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖} \\  & =\frac{({e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2})^{3}}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}{e}^{-3\pi }}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{-\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times 2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖} \\  & =\frac{({e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2})^{3}}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}{e}^{-3\pi }}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{-\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at t=π is R(π)=‖r′(π)‖3‖r′(π)×r″(π)‖=(e−π2)32e−2π=22e−3π2e−2π=2e−π.

R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times 2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖} \\  & =\frac{({e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2})^{3}}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}{e}^{-3\pi }}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{-\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1)$ where $t=0,$ given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=\sqrt{2},$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$
T(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨0,1⟩,$ since the point $P(0,1)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,-1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0,1⟩+\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩+⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve r(t) at the point P(0,1) where t=0, given that ‖r′(0)‖=2, and the unit tangent vector T(t) to the curve is T(t)=22⟨cos⁡t−sin⁡t,−cos⁡t−sin⁡t⟩.

a
The center is ⟨−1,0⟩ and the radius is 2
b
The center is ⟨0,1⟩ and the radius is 2
c
The center is ⟨1,1⟩ and the radius is 2
d
The center is ⟨0,−1⟩ and the radius is 2
e
The center is ⟨−1,0⟩ and the radius is 2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since we are given both the value of ‖r′(0)‖ and the unit tangent T(t), we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature: R(t)=1κ(t)=‖r′(t)‖‖T′(t)‖ Notice that r(0)=⟨0,1⟩, since the point P(0,1) is at the tip of r(0).

Now, we find T′(t), T′(0) and ‖T′(0)‖: T′(t)=22⟨ddt(cos⁡t−sin⁡t),ddt(−cos⁡t−sin⁡t)⟩=22⟨−sin⁡t−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−cos⁡t⟩T′(0)=22⟨−sin⁡0−cos⁡0,sin⁡0−cos⁡0⟩=22⟨−1,−1⟩‖T′(0)‖=22⋅(−1)2+(−1)2=22⋅2=1

Hence, the radius of curvature is R(0)=‖r′(0)‖‖T′(0)‖=21=2.

Next, we find the principal normal vector at t=0 as N(0)=T′(0)‖T′(0)‖=22⟨−1,−1⟩.

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by r(0)+R(0)N(0)=⟨0,1⟩+2⋅22⟨−1,−1⟩=⟨0,1⟩+⟨−1,−1⟩=⟨−1,0⟩.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨0,1⟩,$ since the point $P(0,1)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,-1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0,1⟩+\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩+⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve r(t) at the point P(0,1) where t=0, given that ‖r′(0)‖=2, and the unit tangent vector T(t) to the curve is T(t)=22⟨cos⁡t−sin⁡t,−cos⁡t−sin⁡t⟩.

a
The center is ⟨−1,0⟩ and the radius is 2
b
The center is ⟨0,1⟩ and the radius is 2
c
The center is ⟨1,1⟩ and the radius is 2
d
The center is ⟨0,−1⟩ and the radius is 2
e
The center is ⟨−1,0⟩ and the radius is 2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since we are given both the value of ‖r′(0)‖ and the unit tangent T(t), we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature: R(t)=1κ(t)=‖r′(t)‖‖T′(t)‖ Notice that r(0)=⟨0,1⟩, since the point P(0,1) is at the tip of r(0).

Now, we find T′(t), T′(0) and ‖T′(0)‖: T′(t)=22⟨ddt(cos⁡t−sin⁡t),ddt(−cos⁡t−sin⁡t)⟩=22⟨−sin⁡t−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−cos⁡t⟩T′(0)=22⟨−sin⁡0−cos⁡0,sin⁡0−cos⁡0⟩=22⟨−1,−1⟩‖T′(0)‖=22⋅(−1)2+(−1)2=22⋅2=1

Hence, the radius of curvature is R(0)=‖r′(0)‖‖T′(0)‖=21=2.

Next, we find the principal normal vector at t=0 as N(0)=T′(0)‖T′(0)‖=22⟨−1,−1⟩.

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by r(0)+R(0)N(0)=⟨0,1⟩+2⋅22⟨−1,−1⟩=⟨0,1⟩+⟨−1,−1⟩=⟨−1,0⟩.

solution.reasoning: T'(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle-1,-1\rangle has norm 1. Thus the curvature is \kappa=\|T'(0)\|/\|r'(0)\|=1/\sqrt{2}, giving radius R=\sqrt{2}. The principal normal is N(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle-1,-1\rangle, so the center is P+RN(0)=(0,1)+(-1,-1)=(-1,0). This is option e. feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1)$ where $t=0,$ given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=\sqrt{2},$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$
T(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨0,1⟩,$ since the point $P(0,1)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,-1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0,1⟩+\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩+⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve r(t) at the point P(0,1) where t=0, given that ‖r′(0)‖=2, and the unit tangent vector T(t) to the curve is T(t)=22⟨cos⁡t−sin⁡t,−cos⁡t−sin⁡t⟩.

a
The center is ⟨−1,0⟩ and the radius is 2
b
The center is ⟨0,1⟩ and the radius is 2
c
The center is ⟨1,1⟩ and the radius is 2
d
The center is ⟨0,−1⟩ and the radius is 2
e
The center is ⟨−1,0⟩ and the radius is 2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since we are given both the value of ‖r′(0)‖ and the unit tangent T(t), we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature: R(t)=1κ(t)=‖r′(t)‖‖T′(t)‖ Notice that r(0)=⟨0,1⟩, since the point P(0,1) is at the tip of r(0).

Now, we find T′(t), T′(0) and ‖T′(0)‖: T′(t)=22⟨ddt(cos⁡t−sin⁡t),ddt(−cos⁡t−sin⁡t)⟩=22⟨−sin⁡t−cos⁡t,sin⁡t−cos⁡t⟩T′(0)=22⟨−sin⁡0−cos⁡0,sin⁡0−cos⁡0⟩=22⟨−1,−1⟩‖T′(0)‖=22⋅(−1)2+(−1)2=22⋅2=1

Hence, the radius of curvature is R(0)=‖r′(0)‖‖T′(0)‖=21=2.

Next, we find the principal normal vector at t=0 as N(0)=T′(0)‖T′(0)‖=22⟨−1,−1⟩.

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by r(0)+R(0)N(0)=⟨0,1⟩+2⋅22⟨−1,−1⟩=⟨0,1⟩+⟨−1,−1⟩=⟨−1,0⟩.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=$
questions.worked_solution:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{1}{2} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\sqrt{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ ϕ & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4} \\ {R}^{2} & =1 \\ R & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{3})
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given that the expression $4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)$ can be written as $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ)$ with ${0}^{∘}<ϕ<{90}^{∘}$ and $R>0$, what is the value of $ϕ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=10\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{10}{4} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{5}{2} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: $3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x≈$
questions.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=3 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=4\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{4}{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & ≈0.927\,\text{rad}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(3)^{2}+(4)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =9+16 \\ {R}^{2} & =25 \\ R & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x≈5\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-0.927)
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Given that the expression $\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ can be written as $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ)$ with ${0}^{∘}<ϕ<{90}^{∘}$ and $R>0$, what is the value of $ϕ?$

$ϕ=$ 
{{field-1}}${}^{∘}$
questions.worked_solution:
The sum formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\sqrt{3} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=3\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\sqrt{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ ϕ & =60\,{\,}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=3\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(4)^{2}+(3)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =16+9 \\ {R}^{2} & =25 \\ R & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{1}{2} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\sqrt{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ ϕ & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4} \\ {R}^{2} & =1 \\ R & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{3})
$$

Question 1

32sin⁡x+12cos⁡x=

a
3cos⁡(x−π6)
b
cos⁡(x−π6)
c
cos⁡(x−π3)
d
32cos⁡(x−2π3)
e
2cos⁡(x−π4)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The difference formula for cosine gives

Rcos⁡(x−ϕ)=R(cos⁡xcos⁡ϕ+sin⁡xsin⁡ϕ)=Rcos⁡ϕcos⁡x+Rsin⁡ϕsin⁡x.

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

32sin⁡x+12cos⁡x=Rcos⁡(x−ϕ),

we get the following identity:

32sin⁡x+12cos⁡x=(Rsin⁡ϕ)sin⁡x+(Rcos⁡ϕ)cos⁡x

Equating the coefficients of sin⁡x and cos⁡x, we get the following system of equations:

{Rcos⁡ϕ=12Rsin⁡ϕ=32

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

Rsin⁡ϕRcos⁡ϕ=(32)(12)tan⁡ϕ=3ϕ=arctan⁡(3)ϕ=π3.

Now, we find the amplitude R. Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

(Rsin⁡ϕ)2+(Rcos⁡ϕ)2=(32)2+(12)2R2(sin2⁡ϕ+cos2⁡ϕ)=34+14R2=1R=1.

Note that we only consider the positive root since R>0.

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows: 32sin⁡x+12cos⁡x=cos⁡(x−π3)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=10\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{10}{4} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{5}{2} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=$
question.worked_solution:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{1}{2} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\sqrt{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ ϕ & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4} \\ {R}^{2} & =1 \\ R & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{3})
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

32sin⁡x+12cos⁡x=Rcos⁡(x−ϕ),

{Rcos⁡ϕ=12Rsin⁡ϕ=32

Rsin⁡ϕRcos⁡ϕ=(32)(12)tan⁡ϕ=3ϕ=arctan⁡(3)ϕ=π3.

Note that we only consider the positive root since R>0.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{1}{2} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\sqrt{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ ϕ & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4} \\ {R}^{2} & =1 \\ R & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{3})
$$

feedback.problem: $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\frac{1}{2} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\sqrt{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ ϕ & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & ={(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4} \\ {R}^{2} & =1 \\ R & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{3})
$$

The difference formula for cosine gives

Rcos⁡(x−ϕ)=R(cos⁡xcos⁡ϕ+sin⁡xsin⁡ϕ)=Rcos⁡ϕcos⁡x+Rsin⁡ϕsin⁡x.

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

32sin⁡x+12cos⁡x=Rcos⁡(x−ϕ),

we get the following identity:

32sin⁡x+12cos⁡x=(Rsin⁡ϕ)sin⁡x+(Rcos⁡ϕ)cos⁡x

Equating the coefficients of sin⁡x and cos⁡x, we get the following system of equations:

{Rcos⁡ϕ=12Rsin⁡ϕ=32

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

Rsin⁡ϕRcos⁡ϕ=(32)(12)tan⁡ϕ=3ϕ=arctan⁡(3)ϕ=π3.

Now, we find the amplitude R. Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

(Rsin⁡ϕ)2+(Rcos⁡ϕ)2=(32)2+(12)2R2(sin2⁡ϕ+cos2⁡ϕ)=34+14R2=1R=1.

Note that we only consider the positive root since R>0.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that the expression $4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)$ can be written as $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ)$ with ${0}^{∘}<ϕ<{90}^{∘}$ and $R>0$, what is the value of $ϕ?$
question.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=10\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{10}{4} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{5}{2} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

a
arctan⁡(10)
b
arctan⁡(5)
c
arctan⁡(25)
d
arctan⁡(15)
e
arctan⁡(52)

Incorrect

The difference formula for sine gives Rsin⁡(3x−ϕ)=R(sin⁡(3x)cos⁡ϕ−cos⁡(3x)sin⁡ϕ)=Rcos⁡ϕsin⁡(3x)−Rsin⁡ϕcos⁡(3x)

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

4sin⁡(3x)−10cos⁡(3x)=Rsin⁡(3x−ϕ),

we get the following identity:

4sin⁡(3x)−10cos⁡(3x)=(Rcos⁡ϕ)sin⁡(3x)−(Rsin⁡ϕ)cos⁡(3x)

Equating the coefficients of sin⁡(3x) and cos⁡(3x), we get the following system of equations:

{Rcos⁡ϕ=4Rsin⁡ϕ=10

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

Rsin⁡ϕRcos⁡ϕ=104tan⁡ϕ=52ϕ=arctan⁡(52).

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-10\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=10\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{10}{4} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{5}{2} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the expression 4sin⁡(3x)−10cos⁡(3x) can be written as Rsin⁡(3x−ϕ) with 0∘<ϕ<90∘ and R>0, what is the value of ϕ?

arctan⁡(10)
b
arctan⁡(5)
c
arctan⁡(25)
d
arctan⁡(15)
e
arctan⁡(52)
Submit
Incorrect

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

4sin⁡(3x)−10cos⁡(3x)=Rsin⁡(3x−ϕ),

we get the following identity:

4sin⁡(3x)−10cos⁡(3x)=(Rcos⁡ϕ)sin⁡(3x)−(Rsin⁡ϕ)cos⁡(3x)

Equating the coefficients of sin⁡(3x) and cos⁡(3x), we get the following system of equations:

{Rcos⁡ϕ=4Rsin⁡ϕ=10

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

Rsin⁡ϕRcos⁡ϕ=104tan⁡ϕ=52ϕ=arctan⁡(52).

solution.reasoning: Expanding R sin(3x−ϕ) gives R cos(ϕ)sin(3x)−R sin(ϕ)cos(3x). Matching coefficients yields R cos(ϕ)=4 and R sin(ϕ)=10, so tan(ϕ)=10/4=5/2. Since ϕ is acute, ϕ=arctan(5/2), option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

a
arctan⁡(10)
b
arctan⁡(5)
c
arctan⁡(25)
d
arctan⁡(15)
e
arctan⁡(52)

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

4sin⁡(3x)−10cos⁡(3x)=Rsin⁡(3x−ϕ),

we get the following identity:

4sin⁡(3x)−10cos⁡(3x)=(Rcos⁡ϕ)sin⁡(3x)−(Rsin⁡ϕ)cos⁡(3x)

Equating the coefficients of sin⁡(3x) and cos⁡(3x), we get the following system of equations:

{Rcos⁡ϕ=4Rsin⁡ϕ=10

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

Rsin⁡ϕRcos⁡ϕ=104tan⁡ϕ=52ϕ=arctan⁡(52).

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: $3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x≈$
question.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=3 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=4\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{4}{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & ≈0.927\,\text{rad}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(3)^{2}+(4)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =9+16 \\ {R}^{2} & =25 \\ R & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x≈5\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-0.927)
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=3 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=4\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{4}{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & ≈0.927\,\text{rad}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(3)^{2}+(4)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =9+16 \\ {R}^{2} & =25 \\ R & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x≈5\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-0.927)
$$

EXPLANATION

The difference formula for sine gives

Rsin⁡(x−ϕ)=R(sin⁡xcos⁡ϕ−cos⁡xsin⁡ϕ)=Rcos⁡ϕsin⁡x−Rsin⁡ϕcos⁡x.

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

3sin⁡x−4cos⁡x=Rsin⁡(x−ϕ),

we get the following identity:

3sin⁡x−4cos⁡x=(Rcos⁡ϕ)sin⁡x−(Rsin⁡ϕ)cos⁡x

Equating the coefficients of sin⁡x and cos⁡x, we get the following system of equations:

{Rcos⁡ϕ=3Rsin⁡ϕ=4

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

Rsin⁡ϕRcos⁡ϕ=43tan⁡ϕ=43ϕ=arctan⁡(43)≈0.927rad rounded to three decimal places.

Now, we find the amplitude R. Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

(Rcos⁡ϕ)2+(Rsin⁡ϕ)2=(3)2+(4)2R2(cos2⁡ϕ+sin2⁡ϕ)=9+16R2=25R=5.

Note that we only consider the positive root since R>0.

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows: 3sin⁡x−4cos⁡x≈5sin⁡(x−0.927)

feedback.problem: $3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x≈$
feedback.worked_solution:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=3 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=4\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{4}{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & ≈0.927\,\text{rad}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(3)^{2}+(4)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =9+16 \\ {R}^{2} & =25 \\ R & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x≈5\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-0.927)
$$

Given that the expression $\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ can be written as $R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ)$ with ${0}^{∘}<ϕ<{90}^{∘}$ and $R>0$, what is the value of $ϕ?$

question.worked_solution:
The sum formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\sqrt{3} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=3\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\sqrt{3} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\ ϕ & =60\,{\,}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
The difference formula for cosine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=4 \\ R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=3\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)}^{2} & =(4)^{2}+(3)^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =16+9 \\ {R}^{2} & =25 \\ R & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

links.title: Marginal Distributions for Continuous Random Variables

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}, & \,0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}2y, & \,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint probability density function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\cdot 2y \\  & =3y\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,1]\times [0,1].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}3y\sqrt{x}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}\sqrt{2x}, & \,0\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(y-1), & \,1\le y\le 3 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint probability density function $f(x,y).$

*Hint: We do not know if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.*
questions.worked_solution: Since we don't know whether $X$ and $Y$ are independent, it is impossible to determine the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ using only the given information.

questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}, & \,0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}4{y}^{3}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint probability density function $f(x,y).$

*Hint: We do not know if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.*
questions.worked_solution: Since we don't know whether $X$ and $Y$ are independent, it is impossible to determine the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ using only the given information.

*Hint: We do not know if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.*

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}, & \,0\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}(y+1), & \,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint probability density function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =(\frac{3}{8}{x}^{2})\cdot (\frac{2}{3}(y+1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,2]\times [0,1].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}(y+1), & \,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}(x+2), & \,1\le x\le 3, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{y}, & \,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡4, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(1\le X\le 2,Y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(x+2)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{y} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}(x+2){e}^{y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [1,3]\times [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡4].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{24}(x+2){e}^{y}, & \,1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1\le X\le 2,Y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{1}{24}(x+2){e}^{y}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{24}(x+2)[{e}^{y}]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{24}(x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{24}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2x)]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}(2+4)-\frac{1}{24}(\frac{1}{2}+2) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{5}{48} \\  & =\frac{7}{48}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}x, & \,0\le x\le 4, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}y, & \,2\le y\le 3, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(1\le X\le 2,1\le Y\le 3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}x\cdot \frac{2}{5}y \\  & =\frac{1}{20}xy,\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,4]\times [2,3].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{20}xy, & \,0\le x\le 4,\,2\le y\le 3 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1\le X\le 2,1\le Y\le 3) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{20}xy\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{20}x{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{2}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{8}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(2)^{2}}{16}-\frac{(1)^{2}}{16} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}x, & \,1\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}{y}^{2}, & \,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(X\le 1.5,Y\ge 1).$ Round your answer to three decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}x\cdot \frac{3}{8}{y}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [1,2]\times [0,2].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{2}, & \,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 1.5,Y\ge 1) & ={\int }_{1}^{1.5}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1.5}\frac{1}{4}x{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1.5}\frac{1}{4}x(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1.5}\frac{7}{12}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{7{x}^{2}}{24}]}_{1}^{1.5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7(1.5)^{2}}{24}-\frac{7(1)^{2}}{24} \\  & ≈0.365.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x}, & \,0\le x, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-y}, & \,0\le y, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(0\le X,Y\le 3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & ={e}^{-x}\cdot {e}^{-y} \\  & ={e}^{-x-y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,\infty )\times [0,\infty ).$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x-y}, & \,0\le x,\,0\le y \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le X,Y\le 3) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-x-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{-y}{lim}_{b\to \infty }[{\int }_{0}^{b}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{-y}{lim}_{b\to \infty }[-{e}^{-x}]_{0}^{b}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[-{e}^{-y}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}(x+1), & \,2\le x\le 4, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{{y}^{2}}, & \,1\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(X\ge 3,Y\le 4).$
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(x+1)\cdot \frac{2}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+1}{4{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [2,4]\times [1,2].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x+1}{4{y}^{2}}, & \,2\le x\le 4,\,1\le y\le 2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 3,Y\le 4) & ={\int }_{3}^{4}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{x+1}{4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{x+1}{4}{[-\frac{1}{y}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{x+1}{4}(\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}\frac{x+1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{8}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x)]}_{3}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(8+4)-\frac{1}{8}(\frac{9}{2}+3) \\  & =\frac{9}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
The joint probability density function for the continuous random variables  $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}x{y}^{3},\, & 2\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{X}(x)=2x$ for $x\in [2,4]$

II. $f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Computing the marginal density function for $X,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}x{[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}x,\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $x\in [2,4].$

- Statement II is true. Computing the marginal density function for $Y,$ we get

$$

questions.problem:
The joint probability density function for the continuous random variables  $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}2y{e}^{-3x},\, & 0\le x,\,1\le y\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{X}(x)=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x}$ for $x\in [0,\infty )$

II. $f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Computing the marginal density function for $X,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2y{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{e}^{-3x}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{-3x}(2-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{-3x},\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $x\in [0,\infty ).$

- Statement II is true. Computing the marginal density function for $Y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }2y{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2y{lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{b}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2y{lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x}]}_{0}^{b} \\  & =2y{lim}_{b\to \infty }[-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3b}+\frac{1}{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}y,\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $y\in [1,2].$ So, when $x\in [0,\infty )$ and $y\in [1,2],$ we obtain that 

$$
{{2y{e}^{-3x}}_{⏟}}_{f(x,y)}={{(3{e}^{-3x})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{X}(x)}\cdot {{(\frac{2}{3}y)}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
The joint probability density function for the continuous random variables  $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{X}(x)=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}$ for $x\in [0,1]$

II. $f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
questions.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Computing the marginal density function for $X,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $x\in [0,1].$

- Statement II is false. Computing the marginal density function for $Y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $y\in [0,1].$ So, when $x\in [0,1]$ and $y\in [0,1],$ we obtain that 

$$
{{\frac{3}{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{f(x,y)}\ne {{(\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{X}(x)}\cdot {{(\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2})}_{⏟}}_{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is *not* true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$

$$
\underbrace{\dfrac{1}{4}xe^{-y/2}}_{\large f(x,y)} = \underbrace{\Big(\dfrac{x}{2}\Big)}_{\large f_X(x)} \cdot \underbrace{\Big(\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-y/2}\Big)}_{\large f_Y(y)}.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **independent** if, for all $A\subseteq \mathbb R$ and $B\subseteq \mathbb R,$ we have

$$
P(X\in A, Y\in B)=P(X\in A)\cdot P(Y\in B).
$$

In practice, this is not a very helpful definition when checking for independence since it involves verifying that it's true for all possible subsets $A$ and $B!$

Now suppose that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ and $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y(y)$ are the marginal density functions of $X$ and $Y,$ respectively. Then, it can be shown that $X$ and $Y$ are independent if and only if

$$
f(x, y) = f_X(x)\cdot f_Y (y)
$$

 

for all values of $x$ and $y.$ Notice that this has a direct analogy with the case of independence for discrete random variables.

For continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ whose joint support $S$ is rectangular, we have the following theorem:

*Suppose that the joint support of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ is rectangular. If 

$$

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **independent** if, for all $A\subseteq \mathbb R$ and $B\subseteq \mathbb R,$ we have

$$
P(X\in A, Y\in B)=P(X\in A)\cdot P(Y\in B).
$$

In practice, this is not a very helpful definition when checking for independence since it involves verifying that it's true for all possible subsets $A$ and $B!$

Now suppose that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ and $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y(y)$ are the marginal density functions of $X$ and $Y,$ respectively. Then, it can be shown that $X$ and $Y$ are independent if and only if

$$
f(x, y) = f_X(x)\cdot f_Y (y)
$$

 

for all values of $x$ and $y.$ Notice that this has a direct analogy with the case of independence for discrete random variables.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x, y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y (y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y (y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Joint PDF of Two Independent Random Variables Using Marginal PDFs
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\cdot 2y \\  & =3y\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,1]\times [0,1].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}3y\sqrt{x}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Let X and Y be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

fX(x)={32x,0≤x≤1,0,otherwisefY(y)={2y,0≤y≤1,0,otherwise

Find the joint probability density function f(x,y).

a
 Impossible to determine using only the given information.
b
 f(x,y)={yx,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise
c
 f(x,y)={32yx,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise
d
f(x,y)={3yx,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise
e
 f(x,y)={23xy,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Two continuous random variables X and Y with joint probability density function f(x,y) are independent if and only if

f(x,y)=fX(x)⋅fY(y)

for all possible values x and y, where fX(x) and fY(y) are the marginal probability density functions for X and Y, respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

f(x,y)=fX(x)⋅fY(y)=32x⋅2y=3yx

where (x,y)∈[0,1]×[0,1]. Therefore, the full expression for f(x,y) is

f(x,y)={3yx,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}\sqrt{2x}, & \,0\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(y-1), & \,1\le y\le 3 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint probability density function $f(x,y).$

*Hint: We do not know if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.*
question.worked_solution: Since we don't know whether $X$ and $Y$ are independent, it is impossible to determine the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ using only the given information.

question.html:
Question 2
?

Let X and Y be two continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

fX(x)={382x,0≤x≤2,0,otherwisefY(y)={12(y−1),1≤y≤30,otherwise

Find the joint probability density function f(x,y).

Hint: We do not know if X and Y are independent.

a
 f(x,y)={316(x−1)2y,0≤x≤2,1≤y≤30,otherwise
b
Impossible to determine using only the given information.
c
 f(x,y)={316(y−1)2x,0≤x≤2,1≤y≤30,otherwise
d
 f(x,y)={34(y−1)x,0≤x≤2,1≤y≤30,otherwise
e
 f(x,y)={116(y−1)x,0≤x≤2,1≤y≤30,otherwise
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since we don't know whether X and Y are independent, it is impossible to determine the joint distribution of X and Y using only the given information.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}, & \,0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}4{y}^{3}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint probability density function $f(x,y).$

*Hint: We do not know if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.*
question.worked_solution: Since we don't know whether $X$ and $Y$ are independent, it is impossible to determine the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ using only the given information.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Let X and Y be two continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

fX(x)={3x2,0≤x≤1,0,otherwisefY(y)={4y3,0≤y≤10,otherwise

Find the joint probability density function f(x,y).

Hint: We do not know if X and Y are independent.

a
Impossible to determine using only the given information.
b
f(x,y)={4x2y3,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise
c
f(x,y)={12x2y3,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise
d
f(x,y)={4y23x2,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise
e
f(x,y)={3x24y2,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤10,otherwise
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since we don't know whether X and Y are independent, it is impossible to determine the joint distribution of X and Y using only the given information.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{e}^{2x}, & \,0\le x\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{10}({y}^{2}+1), & \,1\le y\le 2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint probability density function $f(x,y).$

*Hint: We do not know if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.*
question.worked_solution: Since we don't know whether $X$ and $Y$ are independent, it is impossible to determine the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ using only the given information.

choices.value: Impossible to determine using only the given information.

Find the joint probability density function f(x,y).

a

b
 f(x,y)={25(y2+1)ex,0≤x≤ln⁡2,1≤y≤20,otherwise

 f(x,y)={15(y2+1)e2x,0≤x≤ln⁡2,1≤y≤20,otherwise

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Joint PDF of Two Independent Random Variables Using Marginal PDFs

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Joint PDF of Two Independent Random Variables Using Marginal PDFs
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =(\frac{3}{8}{x}^{2})\cdot (\frac{2}{3}(y+1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y)\in [0,2]\times [0,1].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}(y+1), & \,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two independent continuous random variables whose marginal density functions are as follows:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}, & \,0\le x\le 2, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}(y+1), & \,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the joint probability density function $f(x,y).$

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding a Joint Probability for Some Independent Random Variables Using Marginal PDFs
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Joint PDF of Two Independent Random Variables Using Marginal PDFs
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x, y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y (y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y (y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Since our random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =\frac{10}{3{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{4}y \\  & =\frac{5y}{6{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $(x,y) \in \left[2,5\right]\times \left[1,3\right].$ Therefore, the full expression for $f(x,y)$ is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14155486/assets/5f7943e8b9a1bb0f612edf13cc1320e6467781bda7a793f5edefdea660ce4dc4.svg)

Finally, the required probability is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 3,Y\le 2) & ={\int }_{3}^{5}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{5y}{6{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}(\frac{3}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\frac{5}{4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{5}{4x}]}_{3}^{5} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
